name: 3D reconstruction and neural rendering

conventions.text: Draw the scene as a thin wireframe cube (dotted or hairline) with a faded or rendered object inside it, rather than as a box labelled 'scene'; quantities attached to the scene are drawn inside such cubes.
Draw a camera ray as one straight line leaving a small camera glyph (open triangle, camera icon or eye), with the sample points as a row of dots in a contrasting colour along it.
Set the input or source views around the scene cube as photo planes tilted in perspective, with the ray passing through the cube between them.

Show image or plane conditioning geometrically: draw a line from one sample point back onto the image feature grid, source photo or feature plane it reads from, and carry the picked feature onward as a small matching-coloured block.

End a rendering pipeline with a small density-versus-ray-distance plot (sigma on the vertical axis, bare axes, a colour-graded curve) followed by the loss drawn as a coloured predicted-pixel square minus the ground truth inside double norm bars with a squared subscript.
Draw Gaussian primitives as soft, blurred coloured ellipses (never outlined shapes), placed on the rays or in the scene where they live.
Follow two or three individual rays, pixels or samples as parallel colour-coded or numbered lanes through every stage (scene, prediction, rendering) instead of drawing one generic tensor flow.

Make the 3-D representation itself the drawn hinge of the figure (an ellipse cluster, intersecting feature planes, cubes coloured by each quantity) where the arrows meet or turn, while the networks around it stay ordinary boxes.
Shrink the per-point MLP to a small glyph of three or four thin unfilled upright bars, so the geometry and rendering steps take the space.

In a teaser, contrast the prior and the proposed rendering on a single ray: side-by-side panels each opening with the same camera glyph and ray, the prior drawn as plain point samples (or one surface hit) and the proposed geometry (a cone of frustum segments, a set of sampled points against surface bars) added in colour.

source: summarised from the evidence cards listed under each convention
